candidates.label: Sidon (ancient Phoenician port)
candidates.support: An ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, named in the Gospels alongside Tyre as well as in Acts. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the site, continuously inhabited today as Sidon, Lebanon.

summary.text: Sidon was one of the oldest and most prominent cities of ancient Phoenicia, a maritime city with two harbors on the Mediterranean coast. The Gospels record that Jesus withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed the daughter of a Syrophoenician woman, and that he contrasted the repentance Tyre and Sidon would have shown with the Galilean towns that saw his mighty works and did not repent. According to Acts, Paul, delivered as a prisoner to a centurion named Julius for the voyage to Rome, touched at Sidon, where Julius kindly let him go ashore to see friends.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia credits Sidon with leading the Phoenician cities in early seafaring, its sailors said to be the first to sail the open sea by night, guided by the stars, and with becoming distinguished for its manufactures and artisans' skill, including fine metalwork and textiles dyed with the purple later called Tyrian, though the encyclopedia says that dye was earlier produced at Sidon.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records that Sidon revolted against Persian rule in 351 BC, and that the Persian king Ochus then marched against the city with a large army; its citizens are said to have burned their own ships and houses rather than surrender, with a reported 40,000 deaths. The city recovered, and after the death of Alexander the Great it passed to the Ptolemies, the Greek dynasty then ruling Egypt, until 198 BC, when the Seleucid king Antiochus III took it from them; it later came under Rome, which granted it a measure of self-government and the right to mint its own bronze coinage.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Sidon was known for a school of philosophy under the Roman emperors Augustus and Tiberius, and that Berytus's great law school was moved to Sidon after an earthquake destroyed Berytus (modern Beirut) in AD 551. Today Sidon is a city in southern Lebanon and the seat of the South Governorate.

Again he departed from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and came to the sea of Galilee through the middle of the region of Decapolis.

Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.

otConnections.note: Genesis names Sidon as the firstborn son of Canaan in the genealogy of the nations, and describes the border of the Canaanites as running from Sidon toward Gerar and Gaza, and toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Lasha.

During a famine, the LORD sends the prophet Elijah to Zarephath, a town that "belongs to Sidon," where a widow feeds him from a jar of meal and a jug of oil that do not run out, and where he later restores her dead son to life; in the Gospel of Luke, Jesus recalls that Elijah "was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow."

Isaiah's oracle against Tyre names Sidon's merchants as enriching the coast's inhabitants (23:2) and twice addresses Sidon directly, telling the city to "be ashamed" (23:4) and calling it the "oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon" who will find no rest even in Kittim (23:12); Jesus later draws on this same prophetic tradition of judgment on Tyre and Sidon when he says it will be "more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon" on the day of judgment than for the Galilean towns that rejected him.

The LORD commands Ezekiel to "set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against it," declaring judgment on the city by pestilence and the sword so that "they will know that I am the LORD"; this specific judgment on Sidon, together with Isaiah's oracle against Tyre, lies behind Jesus' sayings that it would have been more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon than for the Galilean towns that rejected him.

In an oracle against Tyre, Sidon and the regions of Philistia together, the LORD charges them with plundering Judah's treasures and selling its people to the Greeks as slaves, and promises to free the Judeans sold this way and to sell "your sons and your daughters" in turn "to the men of Sheba, to a faraway nation."

politicalHistory.note: Administers the Cilician plain throughout, and administered Philip's former tetrarchy directly for a few years after his death (34-37; Antiquities 18.4.6).
